rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest and pitchable: “Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike” is a real metric-led angle and explicitly warns not to pretend the rental program caused churn. B has useful bones, especially “Peloton Says It’s Profitable. The Balance Sheet Tells a More Complicated Story,” but it keeps leaning into narrative upholstery like “Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash” and a male CEO assumption the update never earned. A is sharper about decay, proof, and who should not get the pitch; B is close, but looser with inference.
gaps_in_A: “The company everyone wrote off” is defensible as a contrarian frame, but still needs cited prior coverage before it goes into an actual pitch.
“Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike” implies causality the supplied facts do not prove, though the proof section correctly walks it back.
The exec angle depends on “CEO's name and willingness to sit for an interview”; without access, it is a maybe, not a pitchable asset.
gaps_in_B: “What Did He Actually Slash?” invents the CEO’s gender; the update only says “a new CEO.” That is sloppy and avoidable.
“Peloton Is Now Renting Bikes” is inaccurate framing. The update says it is expanding a low-cost bike-rental program nationwide, not launching rentals for the first time.
“Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash” imports a crash narrative not supplied in the update. Prior coverage may support it, but this set did not have that proof.

Angle 2 calls the rental story a “customer-story” and asks for “at least one named subscriber,” but no customer was supplied. That makes it a proof-dependent possible angle, not a clean generated angle.
